To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the introduction and establishment of a marine invader is delayed by a synergism of eutrophica-tion and metal pollution.

(1) disturbance can promote invasions, but a synergistic interaction of multiple disturbances can delay establishment and detection, (2) subfossil assemblage analysis can provide the necessary data to reconstruct the interaction between multiple disturbance factors, and (3) shipping can be a source of invasion in areas that are not adjacent to the native range.
the interaction of multiple environmental factors can shift the selection regime beyond tolerance limits, resulting in significant time lags between establishment and detection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the historical ecology of biological invasions.

(1) the importance of disturbance in promoting invasions, (2) the role of synergistic disturbances in inducing establishment time-lags, (3) the importance of long-term data in reconstructing invasion histories, (4) the importance of subfossil assemblage analysis to reconstruct the interaction between the invasion and the environment and (5) the importance of time lags in invasion ecology.
the interplay between eutrophication, metal pollution and invasion success, and provides a new framework for understanding the history of biological invasions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

eutrophication enabled A. transversas invasion, but the presence of heavy metals prevented its expansion for ~25 years, until a synergistic effect of eutrophization and metal pollution shifted the selection regime beyond the tolerance threshold.

eutrophication, pollution and shipping were the main drivers of this invasion, with eutrophication being the most important factor in shifting the selection regime towards the invasion success of Anadara transvesa.
eutrophication, pollution, and shipping have contributed to the establishment and spread of A. transversas in the Adriatic.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the interplay between eutrophication, pollution and invasion can be reconstructed by subfossil assemblage analyses.
the history of invasion is not only determined by the introduction of the invasive species, but also by the interaction between the species and environmental changes.
the interplay of multiple disturbances can delay the establishment of invasive species for decades.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the quantification of establishment and detection lags in invasions can be crucial for predicting the timing of future invasions, and for understanding their ecological impacts.
the interaction of multiple disturbances can induce time lags in the detection and establishment of non-indigenousspecies, with major implications for the management of biological invasions.
the quantification of time-lags is crucial for the understanding of the invasion process and that the synergism of multiple environmental disturbances may have a major impact on invasion dynamics.
